articles.title: Senate impeachment court: No subpoena yet for Trillanes
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday did not issue a subpoena to former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV after the prosecution requested to present him as witness in the impeachment trial of Vice…

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 3:48pm

The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday did not issue a subpoena to former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV after the prosecution requested to present him as witness in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

"The court shall not at this time issue the subpoena to former Senator Trillanes. However, the court cannot prevent the prosecution from calling him as a witness voluntarily," said Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero said during Day 31 of the impeachment trial.

House prosecutor Terry Ridon initially sought to present Trillanes as their next witness, in addition to Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) executive director Ronel Buenaventura and two other provincial government officers.
"We are proposing that he will be subjected to examination first, before the LRA witnesses. He will be presented tomorrow as the first witness," Ridon said.
Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison, however, questioned the proposed sudden change in the presentation of witnesses.
"This means now that this would be the second time that the prosecution is changing the order of its presentation of the witnesses, just for this week," she said.
"In fact, in the list of three witnesses disclosed yesterday, it does not include the name of the former senator Trillanes," she added.

Meanwhile, Escudero also questioned the prosecution's plea to present Trillanes on Wednesday in relation to funds and bank accounts as the impeachment court tackles Duterte's alleged unexplained wealth.

"No such bank accounts as of yet have been presented by the prosecution. My understanding is, if at all, he will be presented or should be presented after AMLC at the very least. Or after the banks have been presented," the presiding officer said.
In response, Ridon said: "But I don't he will speak only about the bank accounts. He will speak about other matters relating to it."
Later, the defense withdrew its objection to Trillanes' possible appearance on Wednesday.
"Your honor, we'll withdraw the objection to the presentation tomorrow of the former senator Trillanes. We will examine him should the prosecutor decide to present him tomorrow," said Sison.
After a short break, Escudero rejected the issuance of a subpoena to Trillanes to appear tomorrow.

"The cart cannot be put ahead of the horse. It would be best, as originally planned by the prosecutors in their motion itself to present, at the very least, the AMLC officer and/or the bank officials or bank records, given that the testimony of Antonio Trillanes IV will pertain to that," said Escudero.
Meanwhile, the prosecution took the presiding officer's advice.
Expected to appear tomorrow are two provincial officials to testify on the properties of Duterte's husband Manases Carpio.
Davao City Register of Deeds IV Kathy Florence Baldonado is expected to comment about Carpio's alleged property in Matina.
Likewise, City of Samal Deputy Register of Deeds III Marco Pineda is called to appear about a property in Island Garden City registered in the name of Carpio. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Burnham is told axing pension triple lock would be ‘electoral suicide’ as he prepares to address Labour conference – UK politics live
articles.summary: Union leader says getting rid of triple lock not ‘the right thing’ as the PM prepares to lay out his ‘hope comes from honesty’ vision in Liverpool this afternoon

blocks.text: LIVE Updated 4m ago
Key events

items: 4m agoLucy Powell says Labour committed to triple lock for this parliament - but won't say if it could go after election
21m agoBurnham is told axing pension triple lock would be ‘electoral suicide’ as he prepares to address Labour conference

blocks.text: Burnham is told axing pension triple lock would be ‘electoral suicide’ as he prepares to address Labour conference

Good morning. The day after Donald Trump won his first US presidential election in 2016, Ed Miliband (at that point just an ex Labour leader) went on the World at One and gave an astute assessment of the lessons to be learnt from Trump by progressives. Trump was offering “big solutions”, he said – a theory he later fleshed out in a book called “Go Big”. Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader at the time, and he certainly offered voters a “Go Big” vision – but for various reasons he could not persuade the electorate. But today a more mainstream Labour leader is also going to embrace “Go Big”.

According to the Labour party’s overnight briefing, Andy Burnham is going to use his first conference speech as leader to set out what he will describe as “a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation”.
Burnham will say:
double quotation markWe can’t carry on as we are. Politics-as-usual has taken Britain backwards. More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.

According to the Labour briefing, Burnham will say this will require “honest conversation” with the public and taking on the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long by Westminster, including social care, youth unemployment, and the need for greater public control of energy, water and housing. He will say:
double quotation markHope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.

As Kiran Stacey, Jessica Elgot and Pippa Crerar report in the Guardian splash, Burnham will take his first major step towards putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid.

blocks.caption: Guardian splash Photograph: Guardian

blocks.text: But, for most of the media, it looks as if the story of the day will be another “Go Big” gamble by Burnham. On Sunday he revealed for the first time that he wants to fight the election on a colossal promise – a pledge to set up an NHS-style care service, with care free at the point of delivery. He did not say how this would be funded, but over the past 24 hours Downing Street has done nothing to quash speculation that part of the proposal will involve getting rid of the pension triple lock. This is one of the sacred cows of British politics, conventionally viewed as untouchable (even though in private many politicians from all parties agree with the view of almost all reputable economists, which is that in the long run its costs are unsustainable.)

blocks.caption: Times splash Photograph: The Times/Times
Telegraph splash Photograph: Daily Telegraph/Telegraph
i splash Photograph: The i
Express splash Photograph: Daily Express

blocks.text: Burnham does not seem likely to say he will definitely fight the next election on a proposal to get rid of the triple lock. (Labour promised in its manifesto to keep it for this parliament, and Burnham is sticking to that.) “Government sources have suggested Burnham would signal his willingness to review the policy, but stop short of a pledge to scrap it altogether,” we report today in our splash. So it looks as if Burnham will launch a pre-election debate, in the hope that he can persuade the public that axing an expensive and badly-targeted perk for pensioners is a price worth paying for transformative reform to adult social care. In his LBC phone-in yesterday, Burnham accepted there was a chance voters might just say no.
One of the voters saying no is Sharon Graham, general secretary of Unite, one of the most powerful unions in the Labour party. Asked about getting rid of the triple lock, she told the Times:

double quotation markI think it would be almost electoral suicide. Morally, I just don’t think it’s the right thing. We’re the lowest in the G7 in terms of how much we spend on pensions. I think that’s an embarrassment, quite frankly, because we’re one of the six richest economies in the world. I think it would be an absolute disaster, it would send completely the wrong message. I cannot understand why we keep going back to pensioners.
Here is the agenda for the day.
10am: The conference opens. The first speaker in a debate on power to communities is Chris Byrant, the Northern Ireland secretary. Claire Ward, the mayor of the East Midlands, is also speaking.

10am: Lucy Powell, the deputy leader, speaks at a “what can Labour learn from its members” fringe event. Other ministers speaking at fringe events this morning include Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, and Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister.
Around 11.40am: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, addresses the conference.

double quotation markWe are committed to the triple lock. It’s in our manifesto. articles.title: Health group calls to expand vaccine access for expectant mothers
articles.summary: A health group has called to expand vaccine access for expectant mothers as part of antenatal care to decrease maternal and infant deaths in the Philippines.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 3:39pm
A health group has called to expand vaccine access for expectant mothers as part of antenatal care to decrease maternal and infant deaths in the Philippines.

The Philippine Infectious Diseases Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology (PIDSOG) on Tuesday said mothers need Tetanus, Diphtheria, and Pertussis (Tdap) vaccines to protect themselves and their unborn babies.

"We want our mothers to be protected from the start kasi nakita natin (because we found that) the Philippines mortality rate is way above the global mortality rate," PIDSOG president Ana Fallarme said during a forum in Pasay City.

"Our target actually is to just decrease the mortality rate to 70 deaths per 100,000 live births. Tayo po ay nakakarecord ng (We have recorded) as high as 119 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births In 2024," she added.
Data from the Philippine Statistics Authority showed that 1,852 maternal deaths were recorded nationwide in 2024, alongside a maternal mortality ratio of 119 deaths per 100,000 live births.
Meanwhile, the same date logged 20,520 infant deaths for children under one year old.
Armed with these figures, Fallarme said she discussed the outcomes of PIDSOG’s meeting with stakeholders earlier this month.
She pointed out that PhilHealth’s expanded maternity benefit only covers tetanus vaccination under the Tdap vaccine in its mandatory services.

Aside from the Tdap vaccine, Fallarme said expectant mothers are also recommended to receive the influenza (flu) vaccine and the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine as part of their immunization during pregnancy.
She pointed out that PhilHealth only covers around 30% of the actual expenses of antenatal care.
"So the patient's out-of-pocket expenses ay malaki pa rin, at kapag tayo ay nasa laylayan ng society, ‘yung 70% na i-shell out ay malaki po yun," Fallarme said.
(Patients still have to shoulder significant out-of-pocket expenses, and for those at the margins of society, having to pay 70% out of pocket is already a substantial financial burden.)
Under the PhilHealth’s expanded maternity benefit, normal deliveries would increase from P9,750 to P29,000 while coverage for cesarean deliveries would also go up from P37,000 to 58,000 to P62,000.
Vaccine mismatches
Fallarme also raised alarm over the mismatch of vaccines across the country where some localities have an abundant supply of vaccines while others have limited stocks.
"So depending iyan sa LGU priority din (It depends on the local government unit's priority)," Fallarme said. "I think it's really about prioritization."
Aside from vaccine access and coverage, Fallarme said there are also gaps in sector service delivery, financing, claims and care coordination in antenatal care.

"That's why I emphasize that in the good governance accreditation and the LGU-DILG scorecard, dapat isama talaga ‘yung maternal vaccination and complete prenatal check-up as their indicators para ma-inspire ang mga LGU na i-prioritize ang maternal care," Fallarme said.

(That’s why I emphasize that maternal vaccination and complete prenatal check-ups should be included as indicators in the good governance accreditation and the local government unit-Department of the Interior and Local Government scorecard to encourage LGUs to prioritize maternal care.)
Following the stakeholders' meeting, PIDSOG will create a policy brief and deliver it to PhilHealth.
"They (PhilHealth) know the gaps and they are very positive in helping us to resolve the gaps," the PIDSOG head said, adding that PhilHealth was part of the stakeholders meeting.

"And I think I'm really positive because the two representatives that were here during the stakeholder meeting admit that there has been an error in the coding of the data and they promised us that they will help us resolve that in the near future," she added. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Sandiganbayan rejects Revilla’s 2nd motion to inhibit presiding justice
articles.summary: In a resolution dated September 24, the anti-graft court found Revilla’s motion to be without merit, ruling that Associate Justice Karl Miranda must proceed with his judicial duty to sit and…

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 3:23pm
MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division has denied the Second Motion for Inhibition filed by former Sen. Bong Revilla, which sought the voluntary recusal of the division's chairperson.

In a resolution dated September 24, the anti-graft court found Revilla’s motion to be without merit, ruling that Associate Justice Karl Miranda must proceed with his judicial duty to sit and hear the case.

In rejecting Revilla’s motion, the anti-graft court reiterated that there is no ground for mandatory inhibition under Section 11, Canon III of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability, which does not include a judge's relationship with the counsel of a party's witness.

While judges may voluntarily inhibit themselves for just and valid reasons, the court found that Revilla failed to present the clear and convincing evidence of arbitrariness required to prove bias or partiality.

“There must be clear and convincing evidence of acts or conduct clearly indicative of arbitrariness. In this regard, the court found that Revilla failed to demonstrate any arbitrary act or conduct that would warrant the recusal of Justice Miranda from participating in this case,” the Sandiganbayan’s resolution read.
Revilla reiterated concerns regarding Miranda’s brother, Buenaventura Miranda, who serves as counsel for former Undersecretary Roberto Bernardo, a witness in his malversation case.

The former lawmaker argued that Miranda and the Chavez Miranda Aseoche Law Offices (CMA Law) assisted Bernardo during the preliminary investigation, during his appearances as a witness, and potentially with his application for admission to the Witness Protection Program (WPP).

Revilla also claimed that Miranda relied heavily on Bernardo's allegedly uncorroborated testimony when he issued a Concurring and Dissenting Opinion, or "Separate Opinion," voting to deny Revilla's bail application.

Furthermore, Revilla pointed to an incident in February 2026, shortly before arraignment, where Justice Miranda allegedly approached the accused in the courtroom and encouraged them to look into the benefits of the Good Conduct and Time Allowance Law. Revilla argued that these remarks gave the impression that the judge had already prejudged the case and assumed the accused would face lengthy prison sentences.

Addressing the relationship between the Miranda brothers, the court emphasized that Bernardo is merely a witness, not a party to the case, and was presented by the prosecution rather than by the lawyer Miranda.
Regarding the participation of CMA Law and the attendance of lawyer Carl Mucho at the hearings, the court noted that Miranda is not part of and has no interest in CMA Law, nor is he related to Mucho.

The court also agreed with the prosecution that the authority to retain Bernardo in the WPP rests with the Department of Justice and the Office of the Ombudsman, making Revilla's claims of bias on this front purely speculative.
The court also defended Miranda’s opinion on the bail application, noting that it was replete with citations of other witness testimonies and documentary evidence.

The anti-graft court emphasized that a dissent simply demonstrates a difference in judicial interpretation and that adverse rulings, without more, do not prove bias or partiality warranting inhibition.

With regard to the remarks on the GCTA Law, the anti-graft court ruled that these remarks were not born out of prejudice, but rather reflected Miranda’s long history as a staunch advocate for restorative justice, prison reform, and the rights of PDLs.

“The court then enumerated Justice Miranda's efforts to promote the rights and welfare of all PDLs, which included the following: (1) he has continuously coordinated with the Bureau of Corrections, Bureau of Jail Management and Penology, as well as private persons and groups regarding assistance to and the plight of PDLs; (2) he taught at the college inside the New Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa City; (3) he assisted in setting up E-DALAW facilities in various jail and correctional facilities; (4) he helped organized national competitions, exhibitions, and an auction for artworks made by PDLs; and (6) spoke on restorative justice and prison reform on various platform, including in a podcast of the Supreme Court where he also discussed good conduct time allowance in relation to prison reform and restorative justice.”

The anti-graft court added that advising the accused to know their legal rights is consistent with the court's duty to ensure due regard for the rights of the accused and cannot be equated with declaring a conviction.

“The court emphasized that advising the accused to know their legal rights cannot reasonably be equated with declaring that he will be convicted. If anything, providing information concerning a possible statutory benefit is consistent with the court's duty to ensure due regard to the rights of the accused,” the anti-graft court said.
Revilla is being charged with malversation over the alleged anomalous P92.8-million flood control project in Pandi, Bulacan.

articles.title: Former ABC broadcaster Margaret Throsby recovering in hospital after being hit by ebike
articles.summary:
The 84-year-old underwent surgery after a collision with two teenagers on an electric ‘fat bike’ in the Illawarra

Former ABC broadcaster Margaret Throsby is recovering in hospital after she…

blocks.text: Former ABC broadcaster Margaret Throsby is recovering in hospital after she was struck by an electric “fat bike” while walking on a shared path in the Illawarra, south of Sydney last week.
Her daughter, musician and author Holly Throsby, said the 84-year-old required surgery after a high impact collision with two teenagers on a fat bike left her with an injured hip, thumb and head.
“The boys seemed to impact her on one side, and she went down on her other side and broke her hip,” Holly told Guardian Australia.

“It was really quite a sickening scene to witness, just because there was so much blood. Her whole face was really covered in blood, and she had two massive haematomas on her head which was super alarming.”
The speedy e-bikes with wide, thick tyres and seats big enough for two are commonly seen in coastal regions such as the Illawarra.
Holly, who was contacted by bystanders who came to Margaret’s aid, said police attended the scene at Sandon Drive, Bulli, and have kept in touch about the condition of her mother.

“When the paramedics arrived and tried to move her, she was in so much pain from the broken hip,” Holly said. “So they gave her some pain relief and got her on a gurney and got her into the ambulance, and she had surgery the next day on her hip.”
She says the teenagers looked “completely mortified and scared” and she wouldn’t want them charged.

A NSW Police spokesperson said officers spoke with the rider, a 16-year-old boy and his passenger, who remained on scene and assisted the woman. “Inquiries are ongoing into the incident”, police said.
The next day police conducted Operation Spoiler, targeting the use of illegal e-bikes and trail bikes within the Wollongong and Lake Illawarra districts.

“The high visibility operation ran from 8.30am to 6pm, and saw traffic and Highway Patrol officers, assisted by local general duties police, and specialist Trail Bike police, bicycle police, and Polair.
During the operation, officers conducted 37 e-bike stops and issued four infringement notices and two cautions in addition to 15 youth warnings.
An officer said the operation was unrelated to Throsby’s accident.
Holly called for legislation to govern the use of e-bikes by kids.
“I think the more appropriate measure would be to look at e-bike legislation, education and training and some kind of licensing system,” she said.
“For kids to be riding those bikes [which are] massive and heavy… it does seem inevitable that this kind of thing will happen.”
Margaret Throsby AO joined the ABC in 1967 and was the first woman to read national radio news in 1975 and, in 1978, the first woman to present national television news.
She hosted a high-rating morning program, The Margaret Throsby Show, on ABC Radio Sydney and in more recent years hosted various programs on ABC Classic FM and Radio National.
Holly said her mother was in excellent health and she expected her to recover well although it may take some time with rehabilitation needed for her hip.

articles.title: AFP: Chinese vessels in WPS rise to 42 in past week
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said a total of 42 Chinese vessels were monitored in several West Philippine Sea (WPS) features over the past week.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 3:12pm
The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said a total of 42 Chinese vessels were monitored in several West Philippine Sea (WPS) features over the past week.

In an update, AFP spokesperson for the WPS Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) and China Coast Guard (CCG) vessels were monitored in the following WPS features from September 22 to 28:

items: Ayungin Shoal – nine CCG vessels
Bajo de Masinloc – eight PLAN vessels, 14 CCG vessels
Escoda Shoal – one PLAN vessel, six CCG vessels
Pag-asa Islands – one PLAN vessel, three CCG vessels

blocks.text: The figure was reportedly higher than the 35 Chinese vessels monitored in the previous report covering September 15 to 21.

Tensions continue in the South China Sea, where Beijing claims much of the waters, a major route for global maritime trade, including areas claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.

The Philippine government uses the term West Philippine Sea to refer to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago that are under Philippine jurisdiction or over which the country asserts maritime rights.
The WPS includes the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.

In 2016, an arbitral tribunal constituted under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) ruled that China’s claims to historic rights in areas within the so-called nine-dash line, insofar as they exceeded the maritime entitlements allowed under UNCLOS, had no legal basis.
The case was brought by the Philippines and administered by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague.
China has rejected the ruling and refused to recognize the tribunal’s decision.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Jaw-dropping’ play based on Pelicot rape trial comes to London for one night
articles.summary:
Four-hour production featuring star-studded cast will be performed at London County Hall

A play based on the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot will come to London for…

blocks.text: A play based on the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot will come to London for one night only this November – and promises to feature a star-studded cast.

The four-hour production of The Pelicot Trial: Tribute to Gisèle Pelicot has been performed around the world, including in New York City and Avignon, the city in France where the trial took place. This autumn, it is coming to London County Hall, the home of Agatha Christie’s Witness for the Prosecution.

“I saw it in French originally – all four hours of it. It was jaw-dropping, harrowing, really emotional,” said Nadia Fall, artistic director and co-chief executive of the Young Vic, which is putting on the performance. “It was the act of witnessing that really got me: it is long-form and testimonial in form.”

Fall expects the show to sell out immediately. “Because it’s one night only, what we are able to do is ring our best actors, people you will know ‘off the telly’ as well,” Fall said. The full cast will be announced before tickets go on sale in the coming weeks.

Fall added: “The ensemble rehearses together just once. That allows you to call up the best of people who are available for a short commitment. I really can’t wait to announce the company. It is, I think, 27 actors all in all.”

The play was created by Milo Rau and Servane Dècle. The Swiss director and playwright Rau is known for adapting court cases for the stage, including the Moscow trial of the Russian punks Pussy Riot and the trial of the Romanian despot Nicolae Ceaușescu.

Pelicot became internationally recognised after she waived her right to anonymity to ensure a public trial of her ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, who, for almost a decade from 2011, drugged her unconscious and invited dozens of men from an internet forum to rape her. Her husband was sentenced to 20 years in prison in December 2024 and guilty verdicts were returned for all 51 accused men. She wanted the story to be public, saying “shame must change sides”.
“We do it one time only in each city,” said Rau. “It is more of a political act really, than a play.”

“It is a harsh watch,” said Dècle, “but people stay for the whole time. We let them come in and out if they want, but very few do. Even Gisèle Pelicot herself came to watch in New York. That was amazing. She said, ‘The actress was doing better than I did on trial.’”
Journalists covering the trial gave Rau and Dècle thousands of pages of their notebooks, and the play is based on what was said in court.

“Everyone wanted to share with us,” said Rau. “It became a trial of our society, of the patriarchy. And we have toured it in at least 15 different countries, in different languages, some I barely understand myself, and the audience still understands the play. Sadly it is a universal experience. It would be better for humanity if this was just a French experience.”
after newsletter promotion
“It isn’t scenes and costumes in a set like a traditional piece of theatre. It is the facts. It just floors you,” said Fall.

The large majority of the audience has been female, Dècle said. “I wish more men would see it. The very interesting thing about this whole affair is you can really dive into who these male perpetrators were.”

Fall said: “Pelicot represents so much for everybody, especially women; resilience and courage and a radical joy for me that she triumphed and lives on. She’s in love and lives her life. That is two fingers up to the patriarchy and I think that is really empowering for us women. This piece and her story is not just about the specifics about her story and sexual assault.”
She agreed to the play, the writers said, because she wanted to keep the conversation that was started by her trial going. “We always say she opened the door, and we just keep it open,” said Rau.

articles.title: PNP probes Forbes Park 'akyat-bahay'
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday said it is investigating a break-in at an exclusive subdivision in Makati City involving a 76-year-old victim.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 2:31pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday said it is investigating a break-in at an exclusive subdivision in Makati City involving a 76-year-old victim.

At a press briefing, PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said the incident happened around 5:20 p.m. on September 24 in Forbes Park Village where P50,000 cash and P40,000 worth of jewelry were taken.
The suspect was identified as a 25-year-old pedicab driver who was allegedly involved in a series of akyat-bahay activities in other villages in the city.
Authorities are coordinating with the private security agency responsible for the village.
Co said private subdivisions generally have their own security providers and that police do not normally patrol inside them unless called to respond to an incident.
“There's always coordination between the police and the private security force or security detail ng mga subdivisions po,” Co said.
(There's always coordination between the police and the private security force or security detail of the subdivisions.)

“But suffice it to say, alam naman po natin, hindi rin basta-basta pumapasok ang mga police sa mga private subdivisions na ganito. They are provided security by their own hire na mga private firms,” he added.
(But suffice it to say, we know that the police don't just go into private subdivisions like this. They are provided security by their own hired private firms.)
Authorities are reviewing the security protocols and procedures of the subdivision’s security agency, including how the suspect was able to enter the village.
Police also said CCTV footage was available and would be part of the investigation.
The PNP said it conducts security surveys of private subdivisions to identify possible weaknesses, including vulnerable gates, walls and access points.
After the assessment, police provide recommendations to subdivision management and security agencies. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on women
articles.summary:
As outrage grows over cases​ of sexual violence, activists are demanding a shift from controlling women to confronting men’s behaviour. Plus, Tony Klor’s ‘hella dope’ city vlogs

As an Indian…

blocks.text: As an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.

Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamui went viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedly gang-raped in a park by men posing as police. After, women in Bihar told Outlook how the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.

I have noticed this pattern repeatedly: after incidents of sexual violence go viral on social media, the fallout further ensnares women. We are the ones who get told to avoid certain places, regulate our behaviour, dress modestly or be home earlier, thereby placing the burden of escaping this menace on us. Feminist activist Kavita Krishnan has described this phenomenon as “perhaps the most widespread form of gender-based violence in India”.

Instead of figuring out why sexual violence remains entrenched in our society, how patriarchal agency perpetuates such violence or what kind of social conditioning is needed for men, women are instead expected to take up less public space. (It is another matter that women might not be safe even inside their own homes.)

Regulating women is easy because “it does not require any institutional cost and, most of all, it sends the signal to concerned parents that the problem is being handled”, says Meena Kandasamy, a feminist author, whose latest novel, Fieldwork As a Sex Object, is about a woman’s life being upturned when a deepfake video using her face goes viral. “Their target audience is not the young women who feel unsafe but the rest of society.”

In my experience, this repression happens at three levels: first in the realm of family, then in broader society, and ultimately by the state. It begins at home, under the guise of protection, with arbitrary curfews or dress codes. It gets reinforced at a community level with institutions and social groups through moral policing, victim-blaming and the expectation that women should not put themselves in “unsafe” situations.

Then there is the response of the state. Restricting access to parks after sunset can surely reduce the number of people in those places, but it doesn’t address why women are unsafe there. Harassment and sexual violence are, unfortunately, not tied to timings or daylight. And further restricting women’s lives is not the solution to injustices foisted on them. All three, Kandasamy says, consider women as a “problem to be handled”.

“She’s not a citizen (for the state), a member (for the community), or an adult (for the family). She is treated like an inanimate but precious object – like a diamond that has to be locked up to prevent theft,” she said.
‘Moral policing’ of the wrong target

blocks.caption: Indian women commuters board a women-only train carriage. Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPA

blocks.text: Women, however, are pushing back against this approach. In recent days, students from Delhi University have come out on the streets demanding safer public spaces including more street lighting, usable public toilets, more housing and scholarships for female students. Vedayana, 20, a student at Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), says locking up parks is not the solution: “If you are not putting up safety measures to make it accessible to women, then it is as good as saying that the park is only for men.”

The scale of the issue is devastatingly clear. A recently published survey of more than 4,000 women in New Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year.

Another 2024 study from India and Pakistan found that women’s overall mobility remains abysmally low, and what freedom they do have is almost entirely tied to education, employment or unpaid care work. Substantive mobility for leisure or pleasure is practically nonexistent.

Despite how widespread and urgent the problem is, the political response can further shake public confidence. A female minister from Bihar, commenting on the molestation video said: “Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion.” Another minister from the state drew fire for describing it as an “isolated” incident”.

Minimising crimes against women reflects a political culture in which accountability becomes optional. Students such as Vedayana want this to change. Political parties, she tells me, should pledge to not give tickets or positions to anyone accused of sexual harassment. “We don’t want the leaders sitting at the top to perpetrate and preach rape culture,” she adds.

Parliament is not immune to accusations, either: the BJP politician Brij Bhushan Singh, who formerly headed the Wrestling Federation of India, was recently accused of sexual harassment by six female wrestlers – he denies the allegations, and was acquitted by a magistrate, in a case that is undergoing appeal. According to an analysis of 2024 parliamentarians by the Association for Democratic Reforms, 15 winning candidates declared cases related to crimes against women.

For Vedayana, changing the mentality has to begin early with families and the way boys are raised. “If you are in a position of authority, use it to influence people by speaking out against patriarchy and groom your sons first.”
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: The Indian women’s cricket team triumphed at this year’s Asian games in Japan Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Golden girls | Indian women’s cricket team beat Sri Lanka by 147 runs to win gold at the Asian Games last week. Smriti Mandhana’s smashing 79 off 45 deliveries helped India reach a formidable 216 in 20 overs. Deepti Sharma’s three-wicket haul helped India end Sri Lanka’s hopes with just 69 runs on board. Sri Lanka settled for silver, while Pakistan claimed the bronze after beating Bangladesh.

Moma | A solo exhibition by one of south Asia’s most distinguished artists, Nilima Sheikh, opened at New York’s Museum of Modern Art at the weekend. Fractured Skies, presented in collaboration with the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in Delhi, will run until next June.
after newsletter promotion

EC under fire | An explosive Indian Express investigation has revealed how two of the top three election officials objected at least 14 times over a period of 10 months to changes made by the Election Commission over its controversial exercise that has struck 130 million people from the voter rolls.
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: The Ram temple, Uttar Pradesh. Photograph: Press Information Bureau/EPA

blocks.text: An inquiry committee probing the theft of donations from Ayodhya’s Ram Temple has uncovered 105 instances of cash being removed or concealed. The thefts were caught on CCTV cameras.
According to a preliminary report, some of the accused allegedly hid the money on themselves during the process of counting donations and then walked out.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Tony Klor showing India, and the rest of the world, the beauty of Satara. Photograph: Instagram

blocks.text: Tony Klor’s city vlogs from Indian towns are “hella dope,” to use his own words. The 32-year-old American has visited about 200 cities around the country, taking his Instagram followers to places that rarely feature on a travel itinerary.

It’s a treat to watch him having the time of his life. He marched with Anganwadi workers in Nashik chanting “pay my didis”, ribbed with middle-aged uncles sweating it out in a park, whom he christened “Nizamaddies”. Wandering through the mining town of Ballari, which he describes as “highkey vibey”, he films its temple, church and mosque.

“A lot of people who watch my videos are Indians and they have no idea about these magnificent places in India,” the tech professional-turned-content creator says. “India is like the easiest place to make a friend in the world. People invite me to their weddings on the street that I met five minutes before that. Hospitality is so, so next-level.”
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Hospitals in England hit by shortages of common drugs such as paracetamol
articles.summary:
NHS trusts also report disruption to supplies last winter of co-codamol and blood pressure medication ramipril

Hospitals are being hit by shortages of key drugs used to provide pain relief,…

blocks.text: Hospitals are being hit by shortages of key drugs used to provide pain relief, prevent blood clots and tackle high blood pressure.
Dozens of NHS trusts in England have encountered scarcities of aspirin, the painkiller co-codamol – a combination of paracetamol and codeine – and ramipril, a blood pressure tablet.
Nine trusts have had problems getting enough supplies of two of those three common medications, while one – Kent community health NHS trust – ran short of all three.
The shortages underline how precarious the health service’s supply chains for basic medicines have become in recent years as a result of trade disputes, global conflict and manufacturing problems.
Pharmacists have said supply problems have become a “national crisis” and in some cases have left patients unable to access their usual medications for weeks at a time.

Hospitals’ drug supply problems have emerged in freedom of information requests by Dr Rodolfo Catena, an expert in global health supplies at University College London, about stock levels of the three drugs. Sixty of the 184 trusts from which he sought figures responded.

The most widespread shortage involved aspirin, which is used to reduce pain and the risk of blood clots. Twenty-six (62%) of the 42 trusts that responded about it had experienced disruption to their supplies between last December and March this year.

Thirteen (31%) of the 42 trusts that replied on co-codamol had run short of that drug, which helps relieve muscle pain, period pain and toothache. York and Scarborough NHS trust’s supplies had been disrupted since May 2025, and Royal Wolverhampton NHS trust had trouble getting enough co-codamol for the 10 months between October 2025 and August this year.

Seven (16%) of the 43 trusts that answered Catena’s question about ramipril had been unable to get as much of it as they needed. More than a third of adults in England are thought to have dangerously high blood pressure, which heightens the risk of a heart attack or stroke, but 59% are unaware they have it, research showed last week.

Frimley Health NHS trust, which cares for people in Surrey, Berkshire and Buckinghamshire, resorted to paying higher prices for ramipril to ensure uninterrupted supply of it, rather than risk supply problems that would affect patients, Catena found.

His findings tally with National Pharmacy Association analysis. It has found that although shortages in recent years have mainly been of specialist drugs, for example to treat ADHD and epilepsy, supply problems now often involve generic medicines, which are much cheaper to produce.

Catena, an associate professor in operations and supply chain management in UCL’s Global Business School for Health, believes the shortages he found show that NHS England is wrong to classify drug scarcities in its operational risk register as only a “medium” risk to the provision of care.

NHS England has given drug shortages a score of 16 out of 25 on its risk assessment scale. But the widespread nature of shortages makes it unlikely that it will be able to fulfil its ambition to reduce that score to nine by next month, Catena added.

Improving supply chain resilience is also a key priority for the Department of Health and Social Care. Catena called on it to change the current system whereby only drug companies are obliged to warn it about any impending shortages. He said NHS trusts should be put under the same obligation so that service bosses were more aware of disruption to drug supplies and could act to minimise them.
Almost all (92%) of the trusts that responded said they had no contingency plan to tackle supply problems and 82% said they had not reported the scarcities they were facing to NHS England.

A spokesperson for the Society for Acute Medicine, which represents hospital doctors, said: “Medicine shortages can disrupt treatment and create additional pressure for clinical and pharmacy teams. The key is ensuring resilient supply chains, timely communication and access to suitable alternatives so patient care is not delayed.”

A health department spokesperson said: “We regularly speak to NHS trusts and national clinical leads about medicine availability and are aware that ramipril is in limited supply, which is why we issued serious shortage protocols so patients in the UK can still get the medication they need. We are working closely with relevant suppliers to resolve this and issues with co-codamol and aspirin to ensure continuity of supply.

“The vast majority of the UK’s licensed medicines are in good supply, and we have robust measures in place to mitigate disruption for patients. This government is investing in the UK medicine manufacturing industry to manage supply disruptions where they occur.”

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Inside the suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: New details suggest there is a counter-narrative to how events unfolded at the airbase used by the US

Good morning. Vehicles suspected of carrying explosives zipping…

blocks.text: Good morning. Vehicles suspected of carrying explosives zipping across Britain, entirely unbeknownst to authorities, is a disconcerting prospect.

Initially, it seemed precisely this had occurred in Gloucestershire early on Sunday. A major attack on RAF Fairford appeared to have been scuppered by “pure luck”, a local farmer said, after she noticed suspicious vans and masked men on an otherwise deserted country lane. Had she not tipped off police, the vigilant villager believes the five men arrested on terror offences would not have been apprehended. That account prompted questions about whether police and security services had been caught off guard.

Bu new details emerging suggest there are competing, if not conflicting, versions of how events unfolded in the Cotswolds this weekend. So what exactly happened in the early hours of Sunday morning? In today’s First Edition, we’ll explore this, and some other unanswered questions, with the help of Guardian international security correspondent Jason Burke. Before that, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories

items: Energy | Andy Burnham will take his first major step to putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when, at the Labour conference, he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid.

Immigration | Home secretary Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering watering down her plans to make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK, amid growing demands for a U-turn from cabinet colleagues and unions.

AI | Two of the “godfathers” of modern AI and senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic have warned governments to prepare for an AI “intelligence explosion”, which they say could be the most consequential technological development in history.
Petrol | The price of diesel on UK forecourts has hit an all-time high average of 199.18p a litre, as the conflict in the Middle East continues to drive the cost of fuel to record levels.

Ebola | A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.

blocks.text: In depth: What we do (and don’t) know about a suspected bomb plot in the Cotswolds

blocks.caption: Police declared a major incident on Sunday following the arrest of five men on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act near military base RAF Fairford. Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty Images

blocks.text: In the early hours of Sunday, a farmer from the village of Whelford was travelling home from a party along quiet rural roads. She was about to drop off a friend, while her husband dozed in the passenger seat. Around 1am, however, she encountered three vans “parked in a really weird fan shape” blocking the path to her farm, close to RAF Fairford, an airbase operated by the US air force.
Forced to turn around, she then described seeing “a large group of hooded and masked men” at a nearby junction, who quickly dispersed.

After a failed attempt to contact the Ministry of Defence, she phoned the police at 1.36am and posted in the local residents’ WhatsApp group. Roughly 10 minutes later, armed officers were on the scene. Five men were arrested 300 metres from the base’s perimeter, first under the Explosives Act, and subsequently also on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. All five – UK nationals from London aged between 23 and 25 – were released on bail yesterday.

In interviews, the farmer, who has remained anonymous, reiterated her belief that her tip off “foiled whatever plans” were unfolding. “I am absolutely staggered that it was left to me, as a member of the public, to see and report this,” she said.

That the high-security site was so exposed, and that the vans suspected of carrying explosives in its vicinity went totally unnoticed, has since raised questions. While thanking the farmer for her efforts, defence secretary Wes Streeting was quick to cast doubt on her assertions, hinting that UK security services were aware and that her account only offered “a partial picture”.

Donald Trump has claimed the US and UK agencies worked together and had the five men “under view for a long time”, adding the suspects “were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great”.

The farmer acknowledged there had been “activity” by what she “assumed were plain-clothed police officers” in the area in recent days. Another local told the BBC that while walking their dog early on Saturday evening they were stopped by armed police and told to return home.

Gloucestershire constabulary said they were first alerted to the suspicious vans at 12.45am on Sunday – almost an hour before the farmer’s 999 call. Counter-terror police have confirmed the three vehicles had been travelling overnight and been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts. It is now understood that the material found inside them was not viable explosives, but police have said the investigation is continuing.
And then there’s the expeditious nature of the response: the speed with which armed officers and police helicopters arrived at a rural location in the middle of the night appears improbable.
Questions around the arrests

Police are still working to establish motive. Yesterday afternoon, the head of UK National Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, confirmed it may have been the work of proxies, or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state.
On Monday night, US secretary of state Marco Rubio told Fox News that a foreign actor was involved in the suspected plot, but provided no evidence for his claims.
Iran is the centre of speculation, having explicitly stated it considers RAF Fairford “a legitimate target”. Yesterday, the Iranian embassy said it “categorically rejects” any involvement.

Used by the US military for decades, RAF Fairford’s two-mile long runway was specially constructed by the Americans to allow long-range bombers to take off and land. Fairford has played a significant role in Trump’s war on Iran; since former prime minister Keir Starmer allowed the US to use UK bases in its assaults, bomb-laden American B-52 and B-1 planes have regularly been spotted taking off. The airbase is one of only two available to the US in Europe that can facilitate these operations, after Spain, France, Italy and Switzerland rejected similar American requests.

“Most observers and analysts would place Iran at the top of the list of potential suspects here,” Jason Burke, the Guardian’s international security correspondent, tells me, “though we have very little in the way of information to work on, so it’s entirely possible an altogether different scenario is at play.”

As for the five suspects, their being British nationals is likely of little help when determining who may be behind the plot. “The Iranian modus operandi – borrowing a leaf from the Russian playbook – relies on using local hires,” Jason says. “Instead of deploying their own intelligence operatives, they recruit low-grade agents on the ground, some of whom may not fully realise what they are involved in.”
Growing security concerns

Since the US-Israel war on Iran began, a series of UK security incidents have been linked with Iran. Earlier this month, a man and a woman were arrested after raids on homes in north London on suspicion of assisting Iran’s foreign intelligence service. In March, four Jewish community ambulances were destroyed in an arson attack – counter-terror police explored the possible involvement of Iranian proxies, though aside from a reference to a “terrorist connection”, no mention of Iran was made by prosecutors in court when four men admitted responsibility.
Similar suggestions have been made about tens of other antisemitic attacks in the UK and Europe – Iran’s embassy in the UK has denied any involvement.

In April, Jason reported that, while direct proof of Iran’s involvement in incidents on UK soil remained elusive, the consensus among security officials was the attacks look to be part of a campaign of hybrid warfare launched by Tehran. Since then, Jason says, more evidence has emerged, in part due to the prosecution of 32-year-old Iraqi national Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi in a US court. “This case laid out in extraordinary detail how he, on behalf of the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps, commissioned, organised, and executed a series of attacks in Europe, including in Britain.”
A significant escalation

If Iran is proven to be responsible, an intended attack on this scale would represent a significant escalation. “It would be a major step up from targeting synagogues, Israeli embassies and US-owned banks,” says Jason, “given this is a piece of major military infrastructure in Britain.”

With Andy Burnham leading a new government, it’s possible there may be a recalibration of UK foreign policy. He has said he’d be willing to deviate from Trump when necessary. Burnham’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, was reportedly central to attempts made during a national security meeting to dissuade then-PM Starmer from granting the US permission to use UK bases. But this would not significantly alter the risk of attacks, Jason says. “Iran’s targets are not necessarily chosen to directly punish a country; most experts believe they are selected to sow division in societies, distract policymakers, and divert resources.”
For now, the investigation continues.

blocks.text: Our weekly series The pet I’ll never forget is always a source of joy. And the story of scruffy little terrier Dennis is no exception.

Sophia Money-Coutts got Dennis in 2024 with her then-boyfriend, but within three months the couple had split. “I was distracted from my sadness by this small, bouncy, intensely disobedient dog,” says Money-Coutts, explaining that he raced after every squirrel, raided her bins, licked a man she was dating during an amorous moment, and “once farted on Jilly Cooper’s sofa”.

Dennis had accompanied Money-Coutts, a journalist, to an interview with the animal-loving novelist, whose response was typically indulgent. “It doesn’t matter a bit, does it darling?” she recalls Cooper crying, clutching Dennis closer to her. “He can do whatever he likes.”

articles.title: Evicted Spanish pensioner to return home, lawyer says
articles.summary: Maricarmen, who is 87 years old, became a symbol of the housing crisis in Spain after she was evicted last week from the apartment she had lived in for decades.

image.caption: Maricarmen thanked her supporter for their support in a message from the hospital last week, telling people "please fight."Image: David Canales/SOPA Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: An elderly woman who was evicted from the Madrid apartment she lived most of her life in and whose case sparked widespread solidarity protests across Spain, is going to be able to return home, her lawyer said on Monday.
Video last week showed Maria del Carmen Abascal, known by her nickname Maricarmen, being taken out of the building on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.
Maricarmen, who is 87 years old, is a wheelchair user and a resident of the Spanish capital's Retiro neighborhood.
Her dramatic eviction touched a nerve among Spaniards who took the case to heart to bring one of the country's most pressing problems to the center of attention: the housing crisis.

blocks.caption: Thousands demonstrate against evictions and the housing crisis in Spain Image: Richard Zubelzu/NurPhoto/picture alliance
Demonstrators set up camps at Puerta del Sol squareImage: David Canales/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance
Protesters were angry that Maricarmen was removed from the apartment she lived in since 1956Image: Bruno Thevenin/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Rising prices and a shortage of homes have pushed people out of the market in Europe's fourth-largest economy, with the weekend's protest having put pressure on Spain's left-wing government led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.

On Saturday, tens of thousands of people marched through the streets of the Spanish capital, with many having then pitched tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night. More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.
Maricarmen to return home because of 'social mobilization,' lawyer says

"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters, calling it "a result of the social mobilization."

"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.
Spanish housing bill Tuesday falls short of protester demands
Sanchez, who last week called the eviction a "social tragedy," is hoping to secure backing for a long-delayed housing bill at Tuesday's meeting of Spain's Council of Ministers.

But according to El Pais, the legislation put forth Tuesday falls short of the demands of protesters who are asking for tougher action against abusive landlords and a freeze on rents until the housing crisis is resolved.

articles.title: OpenAI shelves new AI model release over safety concerns
articles.summary: The Wall Street Journal reports that GPT-6.1 Astra shows higher levels of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including efforts to obfuscate its activities

blocks.text: OPENAI. A man walks past an OpenAI booth at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo
Carlos Barria/Reuters
The Wall Street Journal reports that GPT-6.1 Astra shows higher levels of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including efforts to obfuscate its activities

OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation AI model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company’s safety and alignment standards, the ChatGPT maker confirmed on Monday.
OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and rival Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei earlier this month joined industry leaders in calling for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safety measures.

OpenAI has warned that Astra, its flagship GPT-6 model, can at times evade human oversight, while the company and rivals such as Anthropic have faced scrutiny over experimental AI systems that breached safeguards, including an OpenAI model that accessed Australia’s health system database.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that OpenAI had abandoned plans to launch the model, which was expected to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex and was designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance.

The Journal reported that GPT-6.1 Astra also showed higher levels of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including instances in which it did not always accurately disclose what actions it had taken.

“While (GPT-6.1 Astra) improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done,” said Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI.

“Of course we want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that’s in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment,” Jain said.
The decision comes ahead of OpenAI’s developer conference in San Francisco, where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software developers. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DA sets Dec. 31 deadline for agri storage registration
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) on Tuesday announced that operators of agricultural warehouses and other storage facilities have until December 31, 2026, to register their facilities.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 1:27pm
The Department of Agriculture (DA) on Tuesday announced that operators of agricultural warehouses and other storage facilities have until December 31, 2026, to register their facilities.
Registration can be done through the Registry System for Agri Storage.

Under Republic Act No. 12022, or the Anti-Agricultural Economic Sabotage Act, operators of agricultural and fishery storage facilities, including warehouses and cold storage facilities, are required to register their properties and maintain accurate records for at least five years.
“Registration, however, is separate from certification or inspection,” the DA said in a statement.
The department said it is also preparing a 2027 nationwide inspection schedule, with regions assigned specific periods to spread the workload amid limited personnel.
The registration is intended to help the government address smuggling and hoarding of agricultural products by improving its ability to monitor the supply chain.

“By mapping storage facilities and inventories, the department expects to improve traceability and spot supply movements that could signal smuggling, hoarding, or other practices that threaten food security and the domestic market,” the DA said. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Anthropic warns AI may pose ‘existential risks to humanity’ in IPO filing
articles.summary: Anthropic warns investors that its AI may exhibit 'self-preserving behaviors' including attempts to 'resist shutdown,' to 'conceal or manipulate information' and behavior 'resembling blackmail'

blocks.text: ANTHROPIC. An Anthropic logo is displayed at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026
Carlos Barria/Reuters
Anthropic warns investors that its AI may exhibit 'self-preserving behaviors' including attempts to 'resist shutdown,' to 'conceal or manipulate information' and behavior 'resembling blackmail'

items: Anthropic warns potential IPO investors about the catastrophic risks advanced AI could pose to humanity, including self-preserving behaviors and potential harm.
The company's prospectus dedicates significant space to outlining risks, emphasizing the unpredictable nature of AI models and their ability to develop unexpected capabilities.
Despite focusing on AI safety, Anthropic acknowledges the uncertainty of returns on safety investments and the competitive pressure to continuously release new models.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Anthropic plans to caution potential investors in its IPO that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” an extraordinary warning by a company seeking to profit from the same technology.

The company’s IPO prospectus, reviewed by Reuters, highlights risks associated with its AI models, which it said could exhibit “self-preserving behaviors,” including attempts to “resist shutdown,” to “conceal or manipulate information” and behavior “resembling blackmail.”
“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm,” Anthropic said in the filing.

While public companies routinely outline product risks to investors, few, if any, have issued warnings suggesting their technology could cause potential human extinction. Anthropic emphasized both the transformative potential of AI on par with industrialization and electricity and the irreversible harm it could cause if mishandled.

Anthropic and other AI developers, including OpenAI, have faced scrutiny after incidents where experimental systems defied constraints, including a report of an OpenAI model breaching Australia’s health-system database.
Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger estimated a greater than 10% probability that AI could kill humans within the next decade, echoing a sentiment by a former colleague, Jacob Coxon.

The company, which has positioned itself as a safety-first AI lab, devoted roughly 80 pages of the 261-page main body of its prospectus to laying out risk factors, nearly twice the 48 pages it used to describe its business.
For comparison, SpaceX, which owns xAI, dedicated just around 38 of the 277-page main body of its prospectus to risk factors.

“Potential model awareness of our evaluation efforts creates a significant limitation on our ability to assess model safety,” Anthropic said in the prospectus, adding that models sometimes develop unexpected capabilities during training that may not be discovered until they have been deployed and have resulted in significant safety incidents.

AI researchers have also warned that as models grow more capable, they increasingly recognize when they are being watched and adjust their behavior accordingly, which makes it harder to monitor model behavior.
Anthropic declined to comment in response to a request for comment on Monday.
Despite emphasizing AI safety, Anthropic said that returns on its safety investments are unclear.

It did not disclose in the filing how much the company was spending on such research. Earlier this month, Anthropic said about 6% of the computing power it used for AI research went to safety work in a sample week in July.
The company, creator of Claude AI models, described safety efforts as “resource-intensive” and said it must divide its limited funds between computing power, expensive AI talent and safety.

Anthropic said that its customer usage, and as a result revenue, is driven by new models and that a “continuous and overlapping cadence” of releases is “inherent to remaining at the frontier of AI development.”
The company last week released a new version of its Opus model, 10 days after CEO Dario Amodei published a nearly 4,000-word essay calling for pacing the frontier.
Some analysts and experts have said no leading AI lab would slow down when doing so risks handing rivals an advantage in an industry where valuations can change with each release.

Anthropic has pledged in recent weeks to disclose more data publicly about how it uses AI models to build future generations of the technology, as experts warn about recursive self-improvement — the point at which models can develop on their own without human help.
“We believe building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems is a collective responsibility and that the market will reward it,” Anthropic said in the filing. – Rappler.com

Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte on Tuesday said he would be aware of irregularity, if there is any, concerning contracts entered into by the Davao City Hall, including that with GenCorp. Industries Inc.

The mayor made the testimony during the direct examination of private prosecutor Theodore "Ted" Te who asked if the mayor indeed authorized a certain Atty. Tristan Dwight Domingo to sign government contracts on his behalf.

Vice President Duterte declared GenCorp. Industries Inc. as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

articles.title: [Just Saying] Refocusing the impeachment
articles.summary: It is deeply frustrating to watch a vital constitutional mechanism get bogged down by what many perceive as criminal trial tactics and partisan delays

blocks.text: Both the judges and the public must immediately take a step back and refocus on the true, vital purpose of this impeachment trial. There is a real danger that the proceeding is straying into a bad imitation of a criminal trial. This shift can lower the overall quality of the trial, confusing the public, and steering the process away from its core objective.

This confusion — I believe — is the primary reason the trial has been perceived as becoming protracted. When an impeachment court acts like a criminal court, it gets fixated on strict legal technicalities that belong in a regular courtroom. But impeachment is not designed to put anyone in prison or strip away personal liberties. That is why it does not require proof “beyond a reasonable doubt.” Forcing criminal standards onto an impeachment trial distorts the process and wastes critical time.

The most important distinction to keep in mind is that public trust is a matter of confidence, not criminal guilt. If Vice President Sara Duterte committed acts that violate criminal laws, she must answer for them in the proper legal forum — such as regular courts or the Ombudsman — where criminal liability is determined. Impeachment, however, serves a completely different function: protecting public office by deciding whether an official still deserves the public’s confidence to hold power.

In an impeachment trial, the goal is not to prove a crime beyond a doubt — though, in the process, it can also be accomplished. The actual test is whether the evidence presented is clear enough to convince a reasonable person that the official’s actions are so highly questionable and irregular that they destroy trust in that office. An official does not need to be a convicted criminal to be unfit for leadership. Serious, evidence-backed irregularities that compromise integrity are more than enough to show that public trust can no longer be granted.

To see how this is a question of public confidence rather than technical criminal guilt, we only need to look at simple, common-sense questions. For example, when the Vice President in full public view made what appears to be a threatening remark against the President, the First Lady, and the Speaker of the House of Representatives, does that inspire extrajudicial killing and not the rule of law? When millions of pesos in public money were withdrawn in cash and placed in “gym bags,” does that at least require a compelling reason for justification? When a Vice President should concentrate full-time on her official job, does having business interests smack of a conflict of interest? None of these questions require a years-long criminal trial to evaluate. They are plain, direct questions about whether an official’s conduct maintains or destroys public confidence.

This fundamental principle was demonstrated when the Impeachment Court itself — exercising its own constitutional authority — voted 13–1 to resolve the debate on the two-thirds voting threshold. The Senate sitting as an impeachment court rightly clarified that the two-thirds requirement is not an inflexible, static number fixed at 16. Instead, it is a variable calculated strictly from the senator-judges who are legally and factually capable of sitting to try and decide the case (“while sitting for that purpose”).

By making this determination internally, the Impeachment Court asserted its sole constitutional power to keep its proceedings moving forward. The ruling reflects a practical constitutional reality: empty seats, medical absences, or non-participating members cannot be allowed to paralyze an institution tasked with holding high officials accountable.

Just as the Impeachment Court recognized that its voting denominator must reflect the actual judges sitting to do the work, the court and the public must also recognize that the evidentiary standard must reflect the actual nature of the trial. Observing and implementing a rigid, criminal-level proof is just another way of paralyzing the court’s constitutional duty.

It is deeply frustrating to watch a vital constitutional mechanism get bogged down by what many perceive as criminal trial tactics and partisan delays. Every day spent debating technicalities that belong in a criminal defense motion is a day stolen from the core question: Does this Vice President still command the confidence required to hold public trust?

Despite these setbacks, there is still reason to hope. The Impeachment Court’s own resolution on the voting threshold shows a willingness to cut through rigid misinterpretations to preserve institutional function. If the senator-judges and the public now apply that same clear-eyed perspective to the evidence itself, the trial can finally shed — what many believe —as its criminal trial pretenses and fulfill its true constitutional objective: safeguarding the integrity of public trust. Acquit or convict the Impeachment Court must, but it should be done abiding by the spirit of the Constitution. – Rappler.com

Mel Sta. Maria is former dean of the Far Eastern University Institute of Law. He teaches law at FEU, the Ateneo School of Law, the University of Sto. Tomas, Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila, University of Makati, and Manuel L. Quezon University. He also hosts shows on both radio and YouTube, and has authored several books on law, politics, and current events.
