image.caption: A screenshot of a video shows members of the white nationalist group Second Sons gathering on the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve near Kamloops, B.C., on Sunday. (@bmorinstories/Instagram)

blocks.text: British Columbia

B.C. politicians and leaders are denouncing a gathering of white nationalists on the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve near Kamloops, B.C. Kúkpi7 Rosanne Casimir said the nation received reports Sunday morning of about 20 to 30 masked men on the reserve.
B.C. politicians and leaders condemn gathering, calling it 'disgraceful' and 'hateful'
B.C. politicians and leaders are denouncing a gathering of white nationalists on the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve, just east of Kamloops.

Kúkpi7 (Chief) Rosanne Casimir told CBC News on Sunday the nation had received reports that morning of a gathering of about 20 to 30 men, wearing white face masks and black caps, standing together around the reserve while hoisting flags over their shoulders.

In a news release, Casimir said "individuals associated with Second Sons Canada, a group linked to white supremacist and white nationalist ideology, have been seen and documented within our community.
"White supremacy will not instill fear in generations of survivors and intergenerational survivors who have already carried fear for far too long."

items: Leaders in B.C. release joint statement condemning anti-Indigenous racism

blocks.text: CBC News has verified that video circulating on social media of the gathering is authentic and depicts members of the group Second Sons Canada on the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve.
Casimir said the reserve's security told the men they were not permitted to gather and asked them to leave. However, they did not leave until RCMP were called and arrived at the scene.
'Clearly intended to intimidate': RCMP

Kamloops RCMP's officer in charge, Supt. Jeff Pelley, said in a news release Monday that front-line officers from the Tk'emlúps RCMP detachment received a report of the group near Chief Eli Larue Way around 7:25 a.m. PT.
Pelley said officers immediately engaged with the group, which then left the location and "continued throughout various parts of the city."

"The posting of a banner bearing the words 'got bones,' combined with the use of masks to conceal their identities while making such public statements is a cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division," Pelley said in the release.
Leaders of growing ‘nationalist’ club praise Nazis, say ‘race war is here’
He said the RCMP takes the matter seriously and will "continue to engage the group" as part of its investigation.
He asked anyone with information, photos or video, or anyone with knowledge of future gatherings, to contact the RCMP.
Politicians condemn event
Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke out against the gathering in a social media post on Monday afternoon.
"The cowardly act that took place at Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc yesterday, is abhorrent," he wrote on Facebook.
"It has no place in this country. My thoughts are with everyone who are shaken and hurt by this disgusting display of hate."
Carney said the gathering is a reminder of the shared responsibility to confront the devastating legacy of the residential school system.
"Courageous Survivors shared the truth, so that all Canadians could take up the work of reconciliation."

Speaking at the Vancouver International Airport Sunday afternoon, NDP Leader David Eby said there has been a rise "in this kind of white nationalist behaviour" in B.C., adding that more needs to be done "to fight it."

"This is just disgraceful, disgusting behaviour. It's very clear that these people were trying to intimidate, make people feel fearful," he said, adding that the masked men would face severe retribution if their identities were known.
Lorne Doerkson, interim leader of the B.C. Conservative Party, condemned the gathering in a post to social media.
"The white nationalist gathering on Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc land this morning was hateful and meant to intimidate. It has no place in British Columbia," he said.

items: Anti-Indigenous racism increasing around Powell River, say Tla'amin Nation citizens

blocks.text: CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, in a post on social media, called the gathering "abhorrent."

"Hate and discrimination of any kind are unwelcome in British Columbia and on behalf of all members of Centre BC, I condemn this behaviour and stand in solidarity with the Tkʼemlúps First Nation," she said.
'Not going to deter us': chief
Casimir said the nation's planned events for Truth and Reconciliation Day on Sept. 30 will go ahead.
"We will not be intimidated," she said.
"This is not going to deter us from gathering, reflecting or honouring our survivors and the children who returned home."
But the incident, Casimir said, is an example of a broader problem.
"Everyone should always be concerned because there's so much racism and discrimination out there."
On Monday morning, Casimir told CBC News's Daybreak Kamloops that community safety is the nation's top priority.
She recommended members stay alert and connected, and report any suspicious incidents.
"We're going to continue moving forward and continuing the work of Truth and Reconciliation. And ... if anything, it just reminds us why this work remains so important."
CBC News reached out to Second Sons Canada but did not hear back before publication.
A national 24-hour Indian Residential School Crisis Line is available at 1-866-925-4419 for emotional and crisis referral services for survivors and those affected.
Mental health counselling and crisis support are also available 24 hours a day, seven days a week through the Hope for Wellness hotline at 1-855-242-3310 or by online chat.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.
With files from Tara Copeland

articles.title: France’s far-right National Rally surges in Senate elections
articles.summary:
Marine Le Pen hails ‘historic victory’ as her party and allies win enough seats to form caucus just months ahead of presidential poll

France’s far-right National Rally (RN) party and its…

blocks.text: France’s far-right National Rally (RN) party and its allies have secured a record 14 seats in the rightwing-dominated Senate in elections, effectively quadrupling its number in the 348-seat chamber just months before a presidential poll.
RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen called the results an “historic victory” after they were announced on Sunday. “The results ‌have exceeded our expectations,” she said.
It was the first time the ⁠party had cleared the 10-seat threshold to be able to form a Senate caucus.
Local elected officials vote for new senators for half the upper chamber every three years, each to serve a six-year term.
The far-right party entered the Senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the National Front, and won three seats in 2023.
Le Pen is considering her best chance yet at power in elections scheduled for a first round in April next year when the centrist president, Emmanuel Macron, steps down.
“This is a historic victory, and a major milestone with the formation for the first time of a group in the Senate,” she said on X.
Nine RN senators were elected on Sunday, according to an AFP tally of results, on top of the three who won seats in 2023.
A further two were elected from RN ally Eric Ciotti’s Union of the Right for the Republic (UDR) party.
RN’s president, Jordan Bardella, said the party’s senators would form a group with UDR allies.

blocks.caption: RN president Jordan Bardella (C) poses with supporters in La Seyne-sur-Mer, southern France, on Sunday as the far right won a record 14 seats in Senate elections. Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ciotti quit the rightwing Republicans (LR) party in 2024 after calling for an alliance with the far right.
The upper chamber’s LR president of more than a decade, Gerard Larcher, 77, is expected to be re-elected next week.
The right, centre and leftwing Socialists looked set to remain the three major forces in the upper house, according to initial results.
The hard-left France Unbowed party won a seat for the first time.
Le Pen’s anti-immigration party emerged as the single largest party in the lower-house National Assembly after Macron called snap polls in 2024, although it fell well short of a majority.
With Reuters

articles.title: Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says
articles.summary:
David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island

Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while…

blocks.text: Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday.
David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”

The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn, after a record multi-billion dollar deal was unveiled in December last year.

Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned. At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.

Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself.

Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua.

After Purdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times that the US had no plans to sell arms to China, while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”
Before the interview, Taiwanese deputy foreign minister Chen Ming-chi spoke of the severe military threat China posed.

“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei.
Trump ​has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.
Perdue himself told CNBC ​on Friday that there had been ​no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms ​sales.
With Reuters

articles.title: Mighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91
articles.summary:
Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New York

Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king…

blocks.text: Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king of the world”, has died aged 91.
Francisco, who got his breakthrough in calypso music with his 1956 hit song Jean and Dinah, died peacefully surrounded by his family in New York on Sunday, his family said in a statement.
His death came after a “brief illness,” the statement said without disclosing any other details.
“He was an institution in the entertainment industry, well admired for his skill and finesse as a singer, songwriter and mentor; beloved by many,” Francisco’s family said.

blocks.caption: Mighty Sparrow performs at the Melkweg in 1989 in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. Photograph: Frans Schellekens/Redferns

blocks.text: The Mighty Sparrow will be remembered as “a defining voice of our culture, a master storyteller and a towering figure whose music helped carry calypso from Trinidad and Tobago to the world,” the Trinbago Unified Calypsonians’ Organisation said in a statement.
Born in the coastal town of Grand Roy, Grenada, in July 1935, Francisco was just a toddler when he migrated with his parents to Trinidad and Tobago in 1937.

Trinidad and Tobago is the birthplace of calypso music, and was where the name and persona of the Mighty Sparrow emerged to produce a list of hit songs in the genre: Both of Them, Congo Man, Mr. Walker, The Lizard and many more.

Birdie, as Francisco was also affectionately known, recorded hundreds of songs in a career that spanned six decades. He performed in several countries around the world, including at famous venues such as New York City’s Madison Square Garden.
Throughout his career, Francisco’s goal was to advance the calypso art form, according to Dr Rudolph Ottley, a Trinidadian cultural historian and author.
“The Mighty Sparrow was the supreme entertainer, a cultural revolutionary and one of the world’s greatest Calypsonians,” Ottley told the Associated Press.
Trinidad and Tobago has honored the composer and performer with national awards, and in 1987 the University of the West Indies conferred an honorary doctor of letters on Francisco.

articles.title: Why some Indian civil servants become heroes for doing their jobs
articles.summary: In a system often marked by red tape and exhausting delays, officers seen to be following the rules get adulation.

blocks.text: Among the thousands of civil servants who keep India's vast government machinery running, a small number become unlikely public figures every few years.
Tukaram Mundhe, 51, is one of them.

The commissioner of Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, he has led a series of enforcement drives since taking charge in May. His teams have inspected restaurants and other food businesses, uncovering pest infestations, poor hygiene and expired food.
He has also highlighted large gaps between what hospitals pay for common medical supplies and what patients are charged.

These actions have made Mundhe a social-media celebrity, with videos and images from inspections widely shared online. Hundreds of people have commented that they wished officers like him could be sent to fix food safety concerns in their state.
Mundhe is not alone. In Gurugram, a suburb of Delhi, district town planner RS Batth has won praise for acting against illegal construction and encroachments.
But why are these officials treated like heroes for doing their jobs?

In India, civil servants are responsible for many services people rely on every day, from issuing documents to policing, food safety and healthcare. But many are also accused of delays, bribes and making people run from pillar to post.
So when an official appears to cut through the red tape, the response can be surprisingly enthusiastic.
"What should have been normal has become exceptional," says retired civil servant Kamal Kant Jaswal.
For many citizens, delays, bureaucratic hurdles and indifferent treatment have become so familiar that efficient governance now stands out as an exception, he adds.
Mundhe is not the first official to gain recognition for doing exactly that.
One of the most prominent examples is TN Seshan, who became a household name as India's chief election commissioner in the 1990s for fearlessly enforcing rules.

Kiran Bedi, the first woman to join the officer ranks of the Indian Police Service, was nicknamed "Crane Bedi" in the early 1980s after it was widely reported that she got an illegally parked car belonging to then prime minister Indira Gandhi towed away (it was removed by a sub-inspector who reported to her, who said years later that she supported, external his decision).

Ashok Khemka became nationally known after intervening in a controversial land transaction in 2012, while police officer Neeraj Jadaun was praised for confronting a mob during deadly religious violence in Delhi in 2020.
These stories have made the idea of the "honest" or "no-nonsense" bureaucrat both familiar and rare.
Jaswal, however, points out that thousands of officials in India do their jobs without attracting public attention.
"Their work may not involve much direct contact with citizens, or may simply be less visible."
For ordinary people, however, a visit to a government office is often seen as an exhausting process.
Rajesh Singh, 43, who works at a finance company in Delhi, says he has experienced long waits to get his work done and even longer processes to solve complaints.
"What is supposed to take 24 hours, I have personally experienced being stretched to six months with no guarantee of a positive outcome even then," he says.
But an officer praised for enforcing rules can also face criticism for applying them too rigidly without taking into account ground realities.

Mundhe has been criticised by sections of the food and hospitality industry over his enforcement drives. He has rejected allegations of selective or unlawful action, saying inspections are evidence-driven and licences are suspended only in serious cases.

Batth, too, has faced flak for acting against illegal encroachments, with critics alleging his enforcement is selective and disproportionately affects vulnerable people. In several viral videos, he has said his actions are carried out strictly under town-planning rules.

Jaswal explains a street vendor's stall may be an unauthorised structure in the eyes of the law, but could be a family's only source of income. And in a country where millions migrate to cities in search of work, unsanctioned living spaces could be the only way to find a place to stay.
This tension between the law and economics helps explain why the same enforcement action can be viewed as both lawful and harsh.
Bureaucrats also face challenges of their own while carrying out their duties.

Pushpa Sundar, who briefly served as a civil servant and has written extensively on development issues, says officers can face political pressure and transfers when they refuse to comply with demands.
"They too have families, careers and financial responsibilities and it needs extraordinary courage to risk those things in order to act independently," she says.
She argues that officers need stronger institutional support when they refuse to do something illegal or improper.
Jaswal remembers facing such pressure himself.
In 1974, when he was district magistrate of Uttarkashi in what was then undivided Uttar Pradesh, a senior minister was contesting the state legislature election.
He says he had to turn down a number of demands from the minister as they were against the rules. The minister won the election and Jaswal says he got his "marching orders soon after".
But when he left for his next assignment, people stood in the summer heat for several kilometres on his way to say goodbye.
The relationship between politicians and civil servants, he says, is rarely straightforward.
Many civil servants who seek desirable postings or rely on political support choose the path of least resistance, while standing up to political pressure entails certain costs, he says.
Social media has also changed how quickly an officer can become a public sensation.
An action once limited to a district can now be filmed, shared and viewed by millions within hours.
"Social media can turn an official into a national talking point almost overnight," Sundar says.
That is partly what happened with Mundhe, whose inspection videos have turned routine enforcement into a widely watched spectacle.
Mundhe, however, sees it differently.
Speaking to the BBC last month, he said his actions were driven by public-health concerns and that businesses complying with rules had nothing to fear.
For Mundhe, the attention is beside the point. The rules already exist and his job is simply to enforce them.
But the public fascination is about more than just one officer.
When basic government functions are carried out visibly and consistently, they can seem extraordinary - particularly because so many people have come to expect otherwise.

articles.title: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane Polo
articles.summary:
Hurricane Nolo is moving away from Hawaiian islands but threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists

Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but…

blocks.text: Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted in areas of the island chain still recovering from previous storms.

Nolo was about 365 miles (585km) south-south-west of Honolulu and moving away from the Big Island at about 12mph (19kph). But the Hawaii county civil defense agency said a high wind warning, wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening as Nolo’s maximum sustained winds rose to 115mph (165kph).

Nolo was expected to strengthen further and turn toward the north-west by Sunday night, though the US National Hurricane Center said the storm’s center would remain well south and south-west of the Hawaiian Islands. The storm was expected to approach the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, a national conservation area, early this week.

Forecasters said Nolo’s outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 20in (50cm ) of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands.

“Don’t venture out if you don’t have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down,” said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center.
Heavy rain fell across the southern part of the Big Island on Saturday afternoon, prompting partial closures of one of the main highways linking Kailua-Kona in the west to Hilo in the east.

blocks.caption: Members of the Hawaii army national guard help a resident leave his home as rainwater from nearby Hurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday. Photograph: Gregory Bull/AP

blocks.text: Near Naalehu, at the island’s southern point, National Guard members were seen guiding a man driving through flooded streets as he tried to leave his home during a downpour. More than 120 guard members were activated on the island, part of roughly 400 statewide after the governor issued an emergency proclamation.
Residents are still recovering from Hurricane Lala , which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.

About a dozen people were in the water Saturday morning at Carlsmith Beach Park in Hilo on the Big Island, despite signs saying the strand was closed. Andrea Gill was out for her regular swim before heading back home to hunker down with family.
Shop owners boarded up businesses, and events were canceled. Gill said storms are common, but hurricanes are rare. She was holding out hope that the islands might not get the full impact.
“We’re used to lots of rain. We’re not used to wind. So it’s always a blessing when we don’t get the wind from the hurricane,” Gill said.
Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to coordinate assistance and provide funding support.
Hawaiian Electric, the state’s primary utility, said crews helping restore power in Kauai after this month’s Hurricane Lowell returned to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in response to Nolo.

The Pacific has been unusually active this season, according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec, with storm activity running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. He said that pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.

blocks.caption: Yellow tapes on Medano Beach on Sunday as Hurricane Polo approaches Baja California Sur, in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. Photograph: Raquel Cunha/Reuters

blocks.text: Meanwhile, parts of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula awaited the arrival of another major hurricane with a similar name, Polo, as it edged closer after lashing other parts of the country’s southwest coast with rain and strong winds.

Hurricane Polo remained a dangerous category 3 hurricane with top sustained winds of 125mph (205kph) and was moving to the north-north-west at 12mph (19kph) about 275 miles (445km) south-south-west of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, US hurricane forecasters said Sunday afternoon. It was moving to the north at 12mph (19kph).
Mexico’s National Meteorological Service, or SMN, said in a post on the social media platform X that Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday.
Mexico’s government issued a hurricane warning along the coast of mainland Mexico from Huatabampito to Guaymas.

The Mexican navy said in a statement that it has gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlan, on Mexico’s Pacific coast, and has deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the hurricane.

One of the towns in the hurricane’s projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja’s Pacific coast. The town has only had full-time electricity for a few years, and still experiences frequent outages. There is concern that washed-out roads could block access to the closest medical facility, about 80 minutes away in Ciudad Constitucion.
“Our people are concerned about this event,” said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel. “We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years.”

Robles Meza said Sunday that the Mexican Army arrived in San Juanico to prepare a shelter and to provide support for possible emergencies. An electrical crew was also there to prepare for Polo’s arrival.

Also on Sunday, tropical storm Rachel formed well off Mexico’s south-west coast, the Miami-based US hurricane center said. It added that Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 40mph (65kph) and was located about 300 miles (485km ) south of Acapulco, Mexico. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect.

articles.title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
articles.summary: In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone the BBC travels to the front line with pro-government soldiers.

blocks.text: Watch: Correspondent takes cover as approaching drone interrupts report
ByNawal Al-Maghafi
Senior international investigations correspondentReporting fromTaiz, Yemen
"This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack."
The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away.
Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed.
It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz.

Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.
We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close.

blocks.caption: Two-panel map of Yemen showing Houthi-controlled territory and contested areas on 24 September. Houthi-controlled territory, shaded pink, covers much of western Yemen including Sanaa and extends south along the Red Sea coast towards the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Purple-striped areas mark contested te…

blocks.text: Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting.
It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire.
"Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ali has remained at home under mortar fire to look after his goats

blocks.text: Image source, Liam Weir/BBC
Ali has remained at home under mortar fire to look after his goats
He told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals.
"I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway."

He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too.

At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach.
"We shoot over them, but we can't pull them out," he said.

Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled.

The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region.

blocks.caption: Detailed map of Taiz in south-western Yemen showing areas of territorial control on 20 September. Houthi-controlled territory is shaded pink and surrounds much of the city, while white areas mark territory outside Houthi control and purple diagonal stripes indicate contested areas.

blocks.text: Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions.

Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha.
We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based.
About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side.

As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle.

We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city.

blocks.caption: Image caption, An international coalition led by Saudi Arabia is providing the Yemeni government with weapons

blocks.text: An international coalition led by Saudi Arabia is providing the Yemeni government with weapons

Taiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.
Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.

Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.
There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line.
"It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said.
The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces.

Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Twelve-year-old Ghana was seriously injured by a mortar while herding goats

blocks.text: Image source, Liam Weir/BBC News
Twelve-year-old Ghana was seriously injured by a mortar while herding goats
In the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied.
Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby.
She lay unconscious, her head wrapped in bandages, her face swollen and bruised. Her family were waiting at her bedside to learn what life might be like if she wakes up.
A doctor told me the injury had damaged her brain. "She will never be the same again," he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The UN says 130,000 people have been displaced by fighting in Yemen so far this month

blocks.text: The UN says 130,000 people have been displaced by fighting in Yemen so far this month
About 20km south of Taiz, at the al-Monig displacement camp, families who had fled Mokha and villages hit by fighting were arriving, among hundreds of tents.
We were told that 200 families had arrived in the previous 10 days.
Maryam Saleh, not her real name, had come a week earlier from Mokha with her husband and five children. The youngest is aged seven. Maryam sat weaving a hat to sell so she could buy food for the day.
"We walked barefoot and we didn't carry anything with us, just our children," she told me.

Her nephew was killed by shrapnel from a mortar as they fled, she said. He had been walking behind her. She described clashes and sniping both ahead of and behind the family and said she then saw armed men on the mountain.
"We thought we were finished," she said. The children were screaming and crying, but the family kept walking, she added.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fatma Mohammed Saleh, who cannot walk, says she crawled for two days before being given a lift by a motorcyclist

blocks.text: Fatma Mohammed Saleh, who cannot walk, says she crawled for two days before being given a lift by a motorcyclist

Fatma Mohammed Saleh was lying on an empty rice sack outside another family's tent. She has a disability and cannot walk, and told me she had nowhere of her own to sleep: "I have nothing… no shelter, no mattress, no family. Nothing."
Fatma said she had been with her two sons and their children when the fighting reached their village. But she was slowing them down so told them to take the children and run, she said.
She spent the next two days crawling on her hands and knees, she said.
"I was crawling and the bullets are coming from here and the shells are there. And the bullets are here, and the shells are here. And above me it was like thunder. I was praying to God."
A man on a motorbike then saw her and drove her to the camp, she said. She has not seen her family since.
On 22 September, the UN refugee agency said more than 130,000 people had been displaced across Yemen so far this month, on top of 5.2 million already displaced by the civil war.
It warned that another 100,000 could – like Fatma – be forced from their homes over the next three months.
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer

articles.title: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war
articles.summary:
Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’

The Trump…

blocks.text: The Trump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”.

Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz.

“They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.”

Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at ⁠the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal ⁠to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said.
Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”.
Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace.
Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”.
Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel.

“Our conditions are clear, ​and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.”
Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country is prepared to resume fighting with the US but has not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal.
“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war.
“At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”

The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for ​talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not ​accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will ​defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
On CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region.

Waltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China premier Xi Jinping during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz.
“I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.”
Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”.

“They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.”

Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating.

“The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.”

articles.title: European cities seek ways of boosting affordable housing
articles.summary: In many major urban centers of Europe, the housing shortage has become an explosive social issue. DW looks into various models that have been put in place across the continent.

image.caption: The Vienna model has provided affordable housing to Viennese residents for more than 100 years Image: DW

blocks.text: In the European Union's most populous city, pressure on the housing market is so great that many of its residents are willing to undertake a historic experiment: Five years ago, Berliners voted in a referendum to instruct the Senate of the German capital to draft a law that would put an end to the power of large real estate companies. Those that owned more than 3,000 units should be expropriated, they said. The Senate did not act on the results of the referendum, which was non-binding. Meanwhile, the average cost of new leases has since risen by about half.

But in the Berlin elections on September 20, the socialist Left Party, which in its campaign had promised to act on the referendum, won the largest share of the vote. Whether it will be able to make good on its promises now depends on how negotiations to form a coalition shape up. But whatever happens, the election has drawn attention once again to the severity of the housing crisis in many cities across Europe.

blocks.caption: Left Party candidate Elif Eralp has promised to be a mayor for all Berliners. Her campaign was largely about providing affordable housing. Image: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Here are some initiatives that have already been put in place:
Vienna: The city is the landlord

The Vienna model is a flagship solution to soaring rent prices in Europe. The ambitious social housing program as introduced after World War I when the Austrian capital experienced a severe housing crisis. Beds were so scarce that some workers had to sleep in shifts. Diseases such as tuberculosis spread in the cramped living conditions.

The model serves to stabilize the city's housing market to this day: According to the Vienna authorities, the city owns approximately 220,000 municipal apartments that it rents out as well as 200,000 subsidized dwellings. More than 60% of Vienna's residents live in one of these two types of housing. This also helps to stabilize prices on the private market.
Public funds in Vienna keep rents down
Basel: Public land, private buildings

The fact that housing is becoming increasingly expensive in many cities is largely due to the fact that a city's attractiveness is reflected in land prices. In many places, people are considering how to decouple rents from the price of land. One means of doing this is not to sell municipal land but to lease it to cooperatives or socially-conscious investors. This benefits councils that do not have to bear construction costs and developers too, as they do not have to factor in exorbitant land costs that are ultimately passed on to tenants.

The Swiss city of Basel is one of the pioneers of this model. About 40% of all cooperative housing units are located on public land. The Spanish city of Barcelona and the Portuguese capital Lisbon have also stepped up efforts to put this model in place.
Paris: Buying back office buildings and converting them into homes

It is harder if land and buildings are in private hands. In 2014, the French capital Paris launched an anti-displacement plan giving the municipality a "first right of refusal" in gentrifying neighborhoods to increase the share of affordable housing in the city. The current target is 30% social housing for low-income residents by 2035

Earlier this year, the French government and the Paris regional authorities identified 61 projects that could convert empty office buildings into housing and create up to 8,200 homes in the inner suburbs of the French capital.

blocks.caption: Certain office buildings in the Paris suburbs are being converted into affordable homes Image: Vincent Isore/IP3press/imago images

blocks.text: Prague: Apartments for public-sector workers

The Czech capital has found another way to keep those without whom the city could not function in Prague: caregivers, police officers, teachers and sanitation workers. Some 660 new energy-efficient apartments reserved specifically for public-sector employees have just been built.

The subsidiary of a Czech bank, which has received European loans, handled the development. The aim is to keep rents 20% below the market rate thanks to economies of scale, and it is not the bank who decides on the tenants but hospitals or public sector agencies, which draw up leases and can attract new employees with affordable rent options. More apartments are currently being planned.

blocks.caption: Few people can afford to live in the center of PragueImage: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Dublin: Non-profit cost rental housing

It has also become difficult for people with low incomes to stay in the Irish capital Dublin. During and after Ireland's financial crisis of 2008, foreign investors bought up a lot of real estate and at the same time rents skyrocketed when several major tech companies chose Dublin as their EU headquarters because of favorable tax rates. There are now long waiting lists for public housing in the city whose supply remains too low.

In 2021, the Irish government introduced the Cost Rental Housing program to provide housing to those on middle incomes, i.e. those who earn too much to qualify for public housing but too little to have a chance on the private market. To qualify in Dublin, a household has to have a net income of below €66,000 ($75,000) per year. Non-profits or public agencies lease out the apartments and rents are below market levels, by an average of almost 30% according to a recent study by the Dublin-based Economic & Social Research Institute (ESRI).

The Irish government hopes to be able to deliver 18,000 low-cost rental homes by the end of the decade. Last year, there were more than 4,200 applicants for 104 apartments in a new community in a suburb of Dublin.
This article was translated from German.
Berlin has space, so why is housing so expensive?

articles.title: Two giant pandas set off to Atlanta zoo from China after Xi-Trump summit
articles.summary:
Pandas departed Chengdu for their new homes in Georgia as part of agreement between Chinese and US governments

Two giant pandas departed Chengdu in south-western

blocks.text: Two giant pandas departed Chengdu in south-western China early on Sunday for their new homes in Atlanta, Georgia, as part of an agreement between the Chinese and US governments.

While in Washington DC for a three-day summit with Donald Trump, Chinese president Xi Jinping announced that the pandas would arrive in Atlanta in the coming days. The loan of the pandas to the Atlanta zoo was one of the few concrete outcomes to come out of Xi’s state visit with the US president, which saw expressions of goodwill between the leaders, but no fixes to any of the longstanding differences between the two countries.
Atlanta said farewell to its last pandas in 2024, leaving the zoo without the bears. The new agreement was announced back in April, but without any dates.

Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are the two adult pandas that will be on loan to Zoo Atlanta for 10 years as part of the agreement. Both pandas were born in 2020 and were kept at the Chengdu research base of giant panda breeding. Ping Ping, the male, has dark black circles around his eyes, while Fu Shuang, the female, has a forehead that protrudes a bit, according to the Xinhua News Agency.
China has long used the pandas as part of its diplomacy globally, deploying the bears in loan programs as expressions of goodwill and letting loan agreements lapse when tensions arise.
Xi had said the loan program was an example of “friendship between the Chinese and Americans”.

articles.title: Ten climbers missing after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp
articles.summary: The Nepali team was preparing to take overseas climbers up the Himlung Himal peak.

blocks.text: At least 10 Nepali climbers who were preparing to lead an expedition are missing after an avalanche hit a base camp in the Himalayas on Sunday.
The climb's organisers said the local guides were at a staging point close to the Himlung Himal peak in Manang district when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning.
Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126 metre (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet.
Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams unable to reach the site.
Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told AFP news agency: "Eight members of our expedition team and two more from another company have been reported missing."
The Nepali team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain.
Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry.
Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches.
The latest death of Nepali climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja.
Extreme weather further south in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said.
It comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August.

More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements.

articles.title: Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
articles.summary: French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic…

image.caption: The pope urged humility and respect for life while addressing the crowd in LourdesImage: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

blocks.text: Around 150,000 attended the Mass celebrated by Pope Leo at the shrine of Lourdes during the third day of his four-day visit to France.

The shrine is venerated by Catholics as a place of healing. Many victims of sexual abuse have also traveled to the site, located near the Spanish border, in recent years as they seek to recover from their trauma.

blocks.caption: Pope celebrated Sunday Mass at Lourdes (pictured) in front of some 150,000 people, following a mass in Paris attended by 800,000 believersImage: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Sunday, Leo urged respect for life, including for the sick and frail, in what was seen as veiled criticism of euthanasia and abortion.

"Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God."
Hundreds of thousands of children abused in France alone

The head of the Catholic Church was due to meet with seven adult survivors of sexual abuse later on Sunday — part of Vatican's decadeslong reckoning with the widespread molestation of children at the hands of the clergy and the steps senior Church figures have taken to cover up the scandal in many countries around the world.
A 2021 report found that around 330,000 children had been abused by Catholic priests and lay leaders between 1950 and 2020 in France.
As pope visits France, sex abuse survivor hopes for healing
While not directly referencing the issue during his Mass in Lourdes, the religious leader called for humility among the clergy's ranks.

"The admission of our mistakes is indispensable for our spiritual growth," Leo told the crowd. "In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze."
But some survivors expressed doubt that the pope's visit would lead to quick changes within the church.
"Things are moving very slowly," Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, a co-leader of a French survivors' association, told the Reuters news agency. "It isn't going to happen overnight."
Pope urges 'vigilance' while meeting bishops

Earlier on Sunday, the pope met with French bishops and praised their "courageous" response to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context."

He thanked the bishops for "listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness and making amends" and praised their "firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."
"You must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance," the US-born pope said, according to the readout provided by the Vatican.

articles.title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
articles.summary:
Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer

Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up…

blocks.text: Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.

Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.

blocks.caption: A community volunteer reminds drivers to slow down to protect baboons in Cape Town, May 2022. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.

Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.

“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”

blocks.caption: A young boy at a protest outside the Urban Wildlife Centre near Simon’s Town on 13 September. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters

blocks.text: Initially, the CBP’s 2025 management plan proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”

The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.
In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.

blocks.caption: A baboon tries to open a car door. The animals often enter cars and buildings and take food.  Photograph: Gallo Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.

However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.
Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.
Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.

blocks.caption: A chacma baboon looking through a windscreen on the Cape of Good Hope. Photograph: Ryogo i Kubo/imageBroker/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.

“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

articles.title: Germany news: Are Germans giving up their beloved meat and sausages?
articles.summary: Germans used to be all about sausages and meat. While those do remain popular, things seem to be slowly changing. There also are new insights into the economic side of East Germany's espionage DW has…

image.caption: A recent study found 93% of households in Germany buy meat productsImage: Maurizio Gambarini/picture allianc/dpa

blocks.text: September 27, 2026
How Cold War espionage helped to boost East Germany's economy

blocks.caption: Karl Marx's economic policies were somewhat helped by the Stasi's foreign espionageImage: Michael Nitzschke/picture alliance

blocks.text: Would you think that espionage could significantly boost a country's economy? In the case of communist East Germany, that seems to have been the case — and to a significant degree.
According to Reuters news agency, a study by the Rockwool Foundation suggests that espionage boosted East Germany's GDP by a whopping 7.4% in the 1970s and 80s.
How, you ask? Well, the notorious Stasi stole scientific and technical information from companies in the West, handed it to companies in the East and helped them increase productivity and growth.

"Stasi espionage strengthened East Germany's ​position within the socialist ‌bloc," said Albrecht Glitz, co-author of the study. "It did not, however, significantly improve success in ​Western markets."

The authors stressed that the East Germany case offers crucial insights for today, as countries again seek to protect strategic technologies, tighten export controls and screen foreign investment in sensitive industries.

articles.title: At least 27 dead in two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
articles.summary:
Seventeen people killed at township bar near Johannesburg and 10 killed in separate incident at store near Cape Town, officers say

Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest…

blocks.text: Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, police have said.

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, south-west of Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.

In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at a store in Lwandle, near Cape Town, at about 1am on Sunday. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.
The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.
No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.

South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.
More details soon …

articles.title: Melbourne man’s mysterious disappearance on popular Peru hiking trail prompts widespread search
articles.summary:
Loved ones describe Jordan Yap, 30, as an experienced hiker who set out for a 10-day solo trek Peru before falling silent

  • Get our

blocks.text: Loved ones of a missing Australian trekker who was last seen nearly two weeks ago on a remote South American hiking trail are urging local authorities to help with the search.

A wide-scale sweep by a private rescue crew has so far failed to find any trace of 30-year-old Jordan Yap, who last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.
He was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains.
Regarded as a very experienced hiker by friends and family, the Melbourne man failed to make contact on Wednesday, his estimated return date.

blocks.caption: Family and friends are urging the Australian government to work with Peruvian officials and local authorities to mobilise further resources in and around the rugged region. Photograph: AAP/Supplied by Kevin Nguyen

blocks.text: He also failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz, where his luggage remains stored, and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco on Thursday.
“It’s really uncharacteristic of him to not have communicated at any point in his journey if he had the chance to,” longtime friend Kevin Nguyen said.
“It is a very popular trek, where you might have 200 to 300 hikers and guides per week during the busy season, so it is very uncharacteristic that no one’s seen him since day one or day two.”
The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.
Local mountain rescue organisation Socorro Andino Peruano has been hired by Yap’s family to help with the search.
His loved ones are holding out hope the rescue group, which recently rescued a Canadian trekker from the same trail, will be able to find him safe.
“Time is of the essence … because ultimately, as much as we were saying he’s been missing since the 23rd, he’s had no contact with anyone since the 14th,” Nguyen said.
Rescue crews completed their biggest day of search operations so far on Saturday (Sunday morning AEST), scouring various trails on the circuit to no avail.
“I know Jordan likes to orienteer and navigate and he’s quite an adventurer himself, so I wouldn’t be surprised if he tried an alternative route,” Nguyen said.
after newsletter promotion
Yap had been planning the trek for more than a year and had recently bought a GPS watch to allow for offline maps to guide him on the hike.
“He was telling everyone about how he was ready to go on a big hike like this, [he was] really excited,” Nguyen said.
He was last known to be wearing a white jacket, green sunshade sweater and grey pants.
The experienced trekker was believed to be carrying a 40-litre hiking bag, Durston dome tent and hiking poles.
Family and friends are urging the Australian government to work with Peruvian officials and local authorities to mobilise further resources in and around the rugged region.
The Australian embassy in Peru is helping his family.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
articles.summary: Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.

image.caption: Tech giant Google has several data centers in Europe Image: Patrick Scheiber/IMAGO

blocks.text: Like coal-fired power plants and wind turbines, few people actually want a data center in their backyard. But they do want to use their services. As a global debate rages about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence, there are also many local discussions about where exactly the data centers needed to train and run AI should be built.

This is currently a major issue in Europe, where many governments and companies have decided that they would prefer to store data in Europe rather than in the United States, which is the global leader in computing. But more digital sovereignty in Europe will mean more consumption of the continent's resources.

According to the German Ministry for Economic Affairs, for every kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed, an average of between 0.4 and 4.4 liters (0.8 and 9.3 pints) of water is used to cool data centers, with the water either evaporating or being diverted back to tanks in a warmed state.
What happens when data centers lose power?
Massive water consumption

The summer that just ended was the hottest on record in Europe — in some areas, water use was restricted for residents, agriculture and even nuclear power plants. The summers are expected to get warmer, so many are wondering about the potential water consumption of data centers in the future.

They are also worried about the high electricity consumption of the centers. Fingrid, Finland's national grid operator, recently forecast that electricity consumption would rise by almost 40% if all projects with signed connection agreements were implemented in full.

This week, the European Commission announced a new scheme for data centers to increase transparency on their energy and water use. Those with a capacity of more than 500 kW will receive an efficiency grade that will also take into account their contribution to the grid, such as the reuse of waste heat. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills," said Teresa Ribera, the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.

blocks.caption: Several data centers are currently under construction in EuropeImage: Maksim Zabarovskii/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Data centers in urban hubs and rural areas

Europe's most powerful data centers have primarily been built near the major cities of Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin (FLAP-D) because of high connectivity, proximity to users and businesses, and well-established ecosystems with specialized engineers and secure supply chains.

However, according to a report by the investment group CBRE, the situation is changing as these markets face power and grid infrastructure constraints. New data centers are being built in the Dutch city of Groningen, Barcelona in Spain or the Belgian capital Brussels, as well as in more rural areas.

And as this happens, there are more and more protests taking place, both on and offline. Earlier this month, hundreds turned up for a protest in front of tech giant Google's offices in the Austrian city of Linz, demonstrating against its already advanced plans to build a data center in the small town of Kronstorf.

blocks.caption: Hundreds protested against a Google data center saying that AI needed democracy Image: APA-Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Earlier this month, bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney successfully led a campaign to overturn planning permission for a proposed data center in the village of Killala, arguing that it would breach national climate policy.

In central France, meanwhile, several elected officials in the village of Etrechet have resigned over Google's plans to build a massive data center, which, at full capacity, would require between 880 megawatts and 1.1 gigawatts of electricity or the equivalent of the total output of a nuclear power plant. Etrechet mayor Florence Laurent told the French daily Le Monde that she was resigning out of a "sense of powerlessness, since the village has no decision-making power" regarding the project.

Some operators of data centers argue that the facilities can be built in such a way that they save energy. A large data center currently being built in Marseille will reportedly use a cooling system that requires 30% less power and consumes no water.
Other data centers, in Scandinavia, for example, use waste heat from the servers and route it into district heating networks via heat exchangers and pumps.

This spring, the German energy company E.ON published the results of a survey that found nearly three-quarters of people would be more likely to welcome data centers near residential areas if they fed their waste heat into the heating network.
Data centers face backlash from US communities

Data center operators also argue that the facilities can serve the public by connecting the batteries that usually provide backup power to local grids so that there is uninterrupted service in the event of power outages or at times of peak demand.
For proponents of building more data centers in Europe, the facilities not only contribute to the continent's digital sovereignty but also help to strengthen energy independence.
Monir Ghaedi contributed to this article, which was translated from German.

blocks.caption: Irish writer Sally Rooney spearheaded a successful campaign against the building of a data center in IrelandImage: Ullstein/dpa/picture alliance

articles.title: US strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not wavering
articles.summary:
Attorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’

While the US secretary of state,

blocks.text: While the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific.

blocks.caption: Ecuador’s president, Daniel Noboa, right, presents the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, with Ecuador’s highest ranking National Order of Merit, the Grand Cross, at Carondelet palace in Quito, on 9 September. Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/AP

blocks.text: On 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador.

“The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added.

blocks.caption: A US patrol vessel intercepting the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador. Photograph: US Southern Command/X

blocks.text: “They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities.

But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US.

blocks.caption: Ten crew members from the five skiffs belonging to the vessel Don Rufo, after they were located and taken aboard the BAE Atahualpa, following air-maritime search and reconnaissance operations conducted by the Ecuadorian navy. Photograph: Ecuadorian Navy

blocks.text: US Southern Command posted an edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny.

It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the latest on 16 September – to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk.

blocks.caption: A still from a video released by US forces intercepting a floating refuelling station supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in the eastern Pacific. Photograph: US Southern Command @Southcom

blocks.text: Also, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”.

Donald Trump has compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday.
Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase.

blocks.caption: Marines and sailors with Maritime Raid Force, LCF-24, boarding the Ecuadorian fishing vessel Conquista 2 in the Pacific on 2 September. Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, South

blocks.text: “Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place.
Noboa has responded with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces.

blocks.caption: Relatives of the four minors apprehended by soldiers and found dead near a military base dance during a rally to demand justice a year after their apprehension in Guayaquil, Ecuador on 8 December 2025. Photograph: Marcos Pin/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: This crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has eroded human rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered.

Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorising joint operations and granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troops taking part in raids last Thursday.

“Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador for the New Yorker magazine.

blocks.caption: People look at the remains of a burned-out fishing boat in the port of Manta, Ecuador, on 6 June 2026. The Ecuadorian national police said at least 20 fishing boats had been damaged.   Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPA
The Ecuadorean army shows drug trafficker Adolfo Macías, alias Fito, being guarded after his recapture in Manta, which is in the Manabi province. Photograph: Ecuadorean Army/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Trump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created called Shield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is a serious contender in October’s election.
So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers.
Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region.

blocks.caption: Fishermen work along the shore as local fishermen are increasingly being pursued by Ecuadorean gangs to move drugs and for their skills navigating the Pacific waters along Ecuador’s coast, in Manta, on 4 June. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters

blocks.text: Isacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”.
